content.title: China overtakes Tesla, ready to mass produce humanoid robots in 2026
content.text:
The US government is reportedly preparing measures to accelerate the robotics industry, including the possible issuance of an executive order in 2026.
From a market perspective, RBC Capital Markets estimates that the global humanoid robot market could reach US$9 trillion by 2050, with China accounting for more than 60%. Several Chinese companies are already preparing to enter the mass production phase, including Unitree, UBTech Robotics, AgiBot, and electric vehicle maker Xpeng.
UBTech, which is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange, is targeting production of 5,000 humanoid robots in 2026 and 10,000 units in 2027. The company also estimates that production costs could fall by 20% to 30% per year, supported by a strong supply chain and local government subsidies.
“The depth of China’s supply chain allows companies to develop and manufacture robots with a significant cost advantage compared with other regions,” said Ethan Qi of Counterpoint Research.


Meanwhile, the United States is considered superior in AI development, autonomy and advanced algorithms. US companies are said to rely on vertical integration to secure performance, safety and intellectual property.
However, the expansion of China’s humanoid robot sector also faces challenges. Dependence on US-made chips, limited AI capabilities in unpredictable environments, and high production costs remain major obstacles.
At present, the cost of a single advanced humanoid robot still ranges from US$150,000 to US$500,000 and needs to be reduced in order to compete with human labour.
In addition, Chinese regulators have begun to warn of a potential investment bubble in this sector. With more than 150 humanoid robot companies offering similar products, the risk of inflated expectations is seen as increasing.
“Many assume that humanoid robots will soon surpass humans in terms of flexibility, speed and autonomy,” said Brauchle.

content.title: china leads humanoid robotics at ces 2026
content.text:
Expected participants include Unitree Robotics, AgiBot, Galbot, EngineAI, Noetix Robotics, and the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre, also known as X-Humanoid, reports China online media outlets. Hangzhou-based Unitree plans to showcase its “next-generation humanoids”, while AgiBot will present its full product lineup.
Last week, Chinese robotics firm UBTech reached a key milestone by producing its 1,000th Walker S2 humanoid robot at its Liuzhou manufacturing facility.
China’s humanoid surge
China’s advances in humanoid robotics are no longer confined to research centers or industrial labs.
In Beijing, humanoid machines are now appearing in retail environments next to common consumer products, highlighting how quickly the technology is entering everyday commerce. This shift from experimentation to commercialization is set to gain international attention at CES 2026 in Las Vegas, where China’s growing influence in the sector will be prominently on display.


Official CES figures show that Chinese companies make up the majority of exhibitors in the humanoid robotics category this year. Of the 38 companies participating, 21 are from China, giving the country more than half of the total presence.
The group includes well-known names such as Unitree Robotics, alongside newcomers like AgiBot and Noetix Robotics, many of which are using the event to pursue international expansion, reports Ajupress.
The size and diversity of China’s showing highlights its growing influence in a sector widely viewed as a critical intersection of advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence.
Industry analysts note that the number of exhibitors suggests a broad, coordinated effort to establish leadership before the global humanoid market fully takes shape.

Chinese companies provided more than 97% of global humanoid robot deliveries in the first half of 2026, significantly outperforming American competitors.

According to research company Smart Analytics Global, about 19.1 thousand such robots were delivered worldwide in six months. This is more than triple the figure for the same period in 2025, when deliveries were approximately 5.1 thousand units.

Analysts forecast that global humanoid robot deliveries will reach approximately 60 thousand units in 2026. By 2030, the market could grow to 500 thousand robots per year.

The largest manufacturer was Shanghai-based Agibot, which surpassed Unitree Robotics from Hangzhou. In the first half, Agibot delivered 8.4 thousand robots and held 44% of the global market. Unitree's figure was 5.9 thousand units.



The volumes of Chinese companies significantly exceed the deliveries of leading American developers, including Tesla, Figure AI, and Agility Robotics. China's advantage is supported by government backing, accessible financing, and rapid expansion of production capacity.

Meanwhile, the number of humanoid robots already performing economically productive tasks remains relatively small. However, the demand structure is gradually changing.

Over 70% of robots delivered in the first half were intended for industrial and commercial use. A year earlier, the share of such orders was about 50%.

In late July, the US banned the import of new Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots, as well as certain components for them. American authorities explained the restrictions were due to risks to the national and cyber security of critical artificial intelligence infrastructure.

content.title: China's Humanoid Robots Are Coming For The US Market
content.text:
The Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas is one of the most prestigious tech expos in the world, often used to debut the most cutting-edge innovations. CES 2026 took place in the first week of January, and 21 of the 38 companies featured in the humanoid robotics category are based in China. The expo highlighted a key difference in mindsets between Chinese and American robotics makers, with the eastern brands promising faster and more affordable results and their western competitors promising greater functionality and data security. Ultimately, the winners of the humanoid robotics race will be determined by consumer sentiment, and it looks like some companies out of China could be hitting the American market as soon as this year.

Meet the Chinese robots that could be coming to America

Of the 21 Chinese companies that presented humanoid robots at CES 26, the most well-known is probably Unitree Robotics. Based in Hangzhou, Unitree already has an established presence in the U.S. 

market, even sold through online retailers like Amazon and Robostore. Unitree used CES to showcase its G1 robot, a humanoid of small stature, standing just over 4 feet tall and weighing just shy of 80 pounds. G1 is very effective at mimicking human motions with great fluidity and genuinely impressive athleticism. Its small size and two-hour battery life present some limitations, but it's already on the market, and at $13,500, G1 beats nearly every competitor on pricing.

One newcomer that made a big splash at CES 26 was Shanghai-based AgiBot, which showcased three humanoids and a robot dog to boot. They covered a range of sizes, beginning with the AgiBot X2, which is about the same height and weight as Unitree's G1, and up to the AgiBot G2, which stands nearly 6 feet tall and weighs over 400 pounds. The company has integrated motion capabilities at the system level, so all three humanoids have a unified design.

El reporte de SAG, citado por Forbes, matiza los números con Agibot en 44% (8.400 unidades) y Unitree en 31% (5.900), pero coincide en el vuelco histórico: Agibot destronó a Unitree como líder mundial.

Cómo Agibot le quitó el trono a Unitree

El detalle clave está en la estrategia de producto. Unitree, la marca más mediática del sector, construyó su reputación alrededor de robots bípedos pequeños y baratos — su modelo G1 acumula unas 7.000 unidades y se ha convertido en el robot humanoide más enviado del mundo, presente en laboratorios universitarios y vídeos virales. Pero Agibot apostó por una gama más amplia: robots bípedos de tamaño completo (serie A), unidades compactas (serie X) y una serie G con ruedas orientada a fábricas y almacenes.

Esa diversificación le permitió a Agibot vender volumen en varios frentes a la vez, mientras Unitree concentraba sus envíos en investigación, educación y demostraciones.

Xataka recuerda que entre 2020 y 2025 se registraron más de 5.600 patentes en China frente a unas 1.500 en Estados Unidos.

"Modelo de mundo": la próxima frontera del software

El cuello de botella ya no es el hardware. El 7 de septiembre de 2026, Unitree presentó el UnifoLM-X2-1.0, descrito por la propia compañía como el primer robot humanoide del mundo impulsado por un modelo de mundo en tiempo real, según Cryptobriefing. Un world model permite al robot predecir cómo se moverán los objetos, cómo responderá su propio cuerpo y planificar la siguiente acción sin control humano remoto.

Esta misma tecnología, llevada al coche, ayudaría a la conducción autónoma a reaccionar ante imprevistos con mayor precisión. Es la convergencia que Elon Musk llevaba años anticipando al definir Tesla como "una empresa de robótica": los coches eléctricos ya son robots con ruedas, y los robots con piernas necesitan el mismo tipo de inteligencia para ser útiles fuera del laboratorio.

At CES 2026, Chinese companies made up the majority of exhibitors in the humanoid robotics category, with 21 of 38 companies coming from China — more than half the total presence. China also leads heavily on volume and IP: Chinese companies provided more than 97% of global humanoid robot deliveries in the first half of 2026, and over the past five years Chinese entities filed 7,705 humanoid-related patents compared with 1,561 in the United States.
